Two things were on my mind. First, I needed something grounding; my calendar’s been a wall of back-to-back roadmap sessions, and scent is the one ritual that flips me from reactive to intentional. Second, I didn’t want to buy another safe bottle just because it’s familiar. The sales associate let me sample Ébène Fumé on blotter first, then on skin. At minute five it softened into this almost meditative palo santo vibe, and I could literally feel my shoulders drop. That somatic cue mattered more than any marketing copy.

Here’s the moment that sealed it: I imagined my 6 a.m. run the next day—humid air, city still waking up—and pictured that scent anchoring me before the chaos. That visualization made the decision; price became secondary. I bought the 50 ml, walked out, and honestly felt a small surge of control return.  

The only hesitation was longevity. Oud Wood lasts a full workday; Ébène Fumé risks fading by late afternoon. I almost talked myself out of it, but realized I was optimizing for edge cases instead of the core need: a morning ritual that sparks focus. If it fades, I can re-spritz after lunch. So I swiped the card, left, and the next morning confirmed it—one spray, quick stretch, and the run felt lighter.

That purchase reminded me how visceral cues—texture of the cap, first inhale, even the heft of the bottle—override spreadsheets of pros and cons. It’s less a transaction, more a micro-commitment to how I want to show up.

history.question: What usually prompts you to look for a new fragrance?
history.answer:
Two things tend to spark the hunt.

First is a mental reset. When I wrap a big product milestone—those all-hands weeks where sleep is optional and Slack never stops—I feel the need to mark the transition back to normal life. Finishing the sprint is great, but it also leaves a bit of residue: adrenaline, loose ends, even a hint of self-doubt about whether we solved the real problem. Picking a new scent becomes a small ritual for closing that chapter. I’ll walk into the Tom Ford counter, spray something unfamiliar on one wrist, then leave and let it linger while I decompress at a coffee shop. If the dry-down still feels like possibility—not pressure—by the time the espresso is gone, I take it home. That’s how Oud Wood joined the lineup right after a launch where we shipped fast but learned we’d misread a key user flow. The smell now reminds me to slow down and listen.

The second trigger is curiosity in the wild. I’ll be running the river loop at dawn, pass someone, and a trace of cedar or vetiver cuts through the humidity. In that split second I wonder who they are, what story they’re carrying. It’s this brief, almost intimate moment that makes me want to decode the note and, maybe, adopt a bit of that energy for myself. I’ll jot a voice memo—“smoky cedar, 6:10 a.m., Marina Bay footbridge”—and later run a quick search or ask a friend in retail to help identify it. The process isn’t about collecting bottles for the shelf; it’s about collecting perspectives. Each new fragrance becomes a conversation starter with myself about who I want to be showing up as the next day.

history.question: Can you walk me through what happens from the moment you decide you want a perfume to actually making the purchase?
history.answer:
The trigger is usually internal—a sense that my current rotation isn’t matching how I want to show up that month. Maybe I’m starting a new project and I want something a bit darker, more assertive. The first thing I do is pull out a little notion doc where I jot quick notes about gaps in my collection: “Need: woody-spicy, less sweet than Oud Wood, works in humid evenings.”

Stage 1 – Online scouting  
I spend an hour or so on Fragrantica and Reddit, toggling between note pyramids and real-world wear reviews. I’ll flag three or four candidates. One mistake I made a couple of years ago was buying off blind-buy hype—lost S$350 on a bottle that smelled great on paper but cloying on skin. Since then I force myself to sample.

Stage 2 – Sampling loop  
Here’s where the emotional roller coaster kicks in. I’ll head to the Tom Ford counter at Marina Bay Sands after work, spray one option on each wrist, and leave. The temptation to buy right there is strong; the lighting, the sales pitch, the packaging—it’s engineered to make you feel decisive. I walk out anyway, run home the next morning, and pay attention to how the dry-down mingles with post-run sweat. If it still feels “me,” it stays on the shortlist; if it turns syrupy, I cross it out.

Stage 3 – Gut check and budget reality  
Usually by the second evening I’m down to one contender. I’ll compare price across Sephora online, the Tom Ford boutique, and duty-free preorders. That comparison used to feel like a chore; now it’s more a sanity check so I don’t pay a 20 % premium out of impatience.

Stage 4 – Purchase  
If the scent still resonates after 48 hours—and my bank app says the month’s discretionary spend isn’t blown—I order through duty-free pickup. There’s a tiny thrill when I unbox it at Changi, but also relief: I avoided another regret bottle.

Pain points that still sting  
• Lack of official 2 ml samples in Singapore. I’d happily pay for them, but SA’s guard those vials like gold.  
• Nose fatigue. After the third test strip I literally can’t smell nuance; it makes decision-making feel shaky.

So, that’s the journey—spark, research, skin test, cool-down period, then swipe. The deliberate pauses are my guardrails against shiny-object mistakes I’ve made before.

history.question: When you try different perfumes, how do you notice their effect on your mood or energy?
history.answer:
The first signal is almost always my breathing. When I spray something like Tom Ford Oud Wood before a morning stand-up, I pause, inhale, and check whether my shoulders drop or my pulse perks up. A dry, smoky note tends to slow me down—there’s a moment of calm, almost like the exhale at the end of a yoga flow. If that happens, I know the scent will keep me grounded through back-to-back meetings.

The flip side came last quarter when I tested a bright citrus blend—felt playful in the store, but at my desk it kept nudging me into distraction. I caught myself jumping between Figma frames instead of settling into deeper work. It took three afternoons of fragmented focus to connect the dots. That little realization was annoying, honestly, because I’d assumed “lighter” equals “energizing.” Turns out my energy spikes only when the fragrance has a bit of resin or spice; too much zest pushes me toward restlessness.

I also watch for how long the effect lasts. After a lunchtime run I’ll re-spray; if the second application still lifts me rather than overwhelming me, the balance is right. Anything that feels cloying post-workout goes straight to the back of the shelf.

What I’ve learned is that mood cues are subtle and physical—heartbeat, breath, even posture—more than some grand emotional wave. I keep a tiny notebook by the mirror and jot a word or two, like “steady” or “scatter,” right after application. Over a month the patterns are hard to ignore, and it guides what I reach for on autopilot each morning.

history.question: Can you recall a time when a fragrance influenced how you felt during the day?
history.answer:
Last November, the team was running back-to-back usability sessions on a new onboarding flow. I knew the day would be long and slightly tense, so I reached for Tom Ford Oud Wood in the morning. 

The first spritz hit with that dry cedar and a faint sweetness. During the cab ride to the office, I noticed my breathing slow a little; it grounded me before I even opened my laptop. Mid-morning, a participant grew visibly frustrated—the prototype kept freezing. In the past, I’d match that tension without meaning to. That day, the scent felt like an anchor; every time I caught a trace of it on my collar I had a small, embodied reminder to stay composed. I kept my voice level, asked a few extra clarifying questions, and the session recovered. 

Around 3 p.m. the usual caffeine crash set in. The fragrance had softened into this warm, almost creamy base. It didn’t re-energize me the way citrus might, but it kept me centered enough to finish synthesizing notes instead of doom-scrolling. By the time I left the office, I realized I’d gone an entire day without that tight feeling in my chest I normally get on heavy testing days. 

Since then I keep Oud Wood in rotation for any scenario where I expect emotional volatility—user testing, roadmap reviews, even difficult 1:1s—because, for me, it dampens the spikes and keeps the baseline steady.

history.question: What sort of feelings or states do you hope to experience when choosing a perfume?
history.answer:
First, I’m after a sense of being anchored. Mornings here move fast—Slack pings by the second—so I reach for something woody and slightly smoky because it settles my nerves before the chaos hits. The moment that top note lands, it’s like, “Okay, Liam, breathe. You’re in control.” I discovered that need during a brutal launch two years ago: I was sprinting on pure caffeine, and a quick spritz of Oud Wood honestly felt like planting my feet back on the ground. That memory stuck, so now grounding is non-negotiable.

The second feeling is quiet confidence—not the extroverted, look-at-me buzz, more an internal click that says I’m prepared to speak up for users even if the room’s skeptical. On days with high-stakes reviews I’ll swap to something slightly spicier, still woody, because the sharper edges keep me alert and, weirdly, a little braver. If I walk into that meeting already smelling like the version of myself I want to be, the words come easier.

Those two states—grounded and quietly confident—guide almost every pick from my shelf. Everything else, projection, longevity, whatever, is just tuning knobs.

history.question: Have you ever avoided or stopped using a perfume because of the way it made you feel?
history.answer:
Yeah, once. About two years ago I picked up a bottle of Tom Ford Grey Vetiver. On paper the notes sounded perfect—earthy, a bit smoky, very “grown-up.” I wore it the week we were pushing a major redesign to production. Long nights, back-to-back stand-ups, a nasty rollback on launch day—the kind of sprint that lives in your nervous system.  

By Friday I caught myself tensing up the moment the scent hit my skin. It wasn’t the perfume’s fault; my body had just welded that smell to the stress spike—elevated heart rate, jaw clenched, the whole thing. I tried giving it space, wore it again a month later before a casual coffee chat. Same reaction: a low, background buzz of anxiety I couldn’t shake.  

That bothered me because fragrance is supposed to be my little ritual for feeling grounded before I face a team. Instead, this one kept yanking me back to that chaotic week. After the second try I shelved it, told myself I’d circle back. I never did. Eventually I passed the bottle to a friend who loves vetiver. Watching him light up when he sprayed it felt oddly cathartic—you know, like I’d let the scent have a new life without the baggage.  

The experience nudged me to pay closer attention to the emotional residue attached to everyday objects. Now, if a fragrance even hints at stress memories, I don’t force it. The goal is energy and clarity, not silent triggers.

history.question: When you reflect on the perfumes you've owned, are there any scents that stood out for their impact on your motivation or confidence?
history.answer:
Oud Wood is the one that really changed things for me. I bought the bottle right before a nerve-racking design review with our VP—fresh team, new product, tons of eyes on me. The first morning I wore it, the dry-down felt like this quiet, almost meditative warmth. I remember stepping into the lift, catching a whiff of the sandalwood, and thinking, “Okay, I can handle whatever shows up in that room.” It wasn’t a loud scent, just a steady reminder to slow my breathing. I still reach for it when a project feels bigger than me; the association is locked in now.

The opposite happened with a very bright citrus-aquatic sample—can’t even recall the name. Early in my career I thought lighter automatically meant more “office-safe.” Instead, I kept noticing how quickly it evaporated; by lunch I’d catch a faint synthetic note and feel… flimsy? That fleeting quality mirrored the way I was second-guessing myself back then. After maybe two weeks I shelved it and realised scent longevity matters to my sense of follow-through.

Those experiences taught me that the fragrance has to mirror the energy I’m trying to project—enduring woods for grounded confidence, fewer airy top-notes when I need staying power. Now I’m more intentional: if I wake up anxious about stakeholder alignment, it’s Oud Wood. If I’m prepping for heads-down wireframing, something slightly spicier like Tobacco Vanille nudges me into flow. It’s become a small but reliable lever for motivation.

history.question: How do you usually decide which scent to wear on a particular day?
history.answer:
Most mornings I pause right after my run—still cooling down, standing in front of the dresser—because that’s when I have the clearest sense of what the day might demand. Two quick checks guide me:

First, mood and intent. I glance at the calendar and ask, “Do I need grounding or lift?” If it’s back-to-back reviews with senior leadership, I reach for Tom Ford Oud Wood. The depth in that scent feels like an anchor; it reminds me to slow my breathing, choose my words. On lighter research or prototyping days, I go with something like Costa Azzurra—the salinity keeps the energy playful, which helps me stay curious with users.

Second, the Singapore weather. Humidity can amplify a perfume in ways that, um, sometimes overwhelm colleagues in small meeting rooms. I learned that the hard way last year when I wore Tobacco Vanille to a workshop—great scent, wrong climate. People kept cracking windows, and I spent the session worrying about my sillage instead of listening. Now I dab rather than spray if the forecast says 32 °C and 90 % humidity.

Those two lenses—emotional intent and environment—usually point me to the right bottle. The ritual takes maybe thirty seconds, but it frames the entire day.

history.question: What role, if any, do memories or associations play when you select a perfume?
history.answer:
Memories sit in the background like an old-school playlist—I don’t consciously reach for them, but the second the cap comes off they flood in and steer the choice.

The strongest anchor is Tom Ford Oud Wood. I first wore it during a nerve-racking board review three years ago. I’d pulled an all-nighter polishing prototypes, walked into the conference room half-awake, and the scent—dry wood, a hint of cardamom—hit before the coffee did. The meeting went better than I’d dared to hope. Since then, that smell is wired to the feeling of “I survived, I can do hard things.” On mornings when Slack is already on fire, I’ll catch myself reaching for it almost automatically. It’s less about believing the perfume is lucky and more about borrowing that visceral memory of composure under pressure.

There’s a softer association with Santal Blush. My partner surprised me with it after my first half-marathon; we celebrated over hawker-stall kopi by the Singapore River, sweat, sandalwood, and slightly burnt toast all mingling in the humidity. When I’m heading into a long afternoon of heads-down design work, that fragrance puts me back on that post-run high—steady heart rate, clear focus. I didn’t plan that link; it just stuck.

I did get it wrong once. I wore Oud Wood to a casual team offsite thinking I’d feel “grounded,” but colleagues joked I smelled like I was about to present Q4 forecasts. The formality of that memory created distance instead of camaraderie. Since then I double-check: is the memory I’m tapping into aligned with the vibe I want to project to others, not just what I want to feel inside? That tiny pause keeps nostalgia from sabotaging the social context.

history.question: Have friends or family ever commented on your scent choices? If so, how did that affect your decisions?
history.answer:
Quite a few times. The one that really stuck happened during a usability test last year. I showed up in Tobacco Vanille—felt confident walking in, that warm, woody-sweet cloud around me. Mid-session, a participant rubbed her temples and quietly asked if we could crack a window. Later she mentioned heavy scents sometimes trigger migraines. I’d been so focused on reading her reactions to the prototype that I’d ignored the possibility my own presence was skewing the environment. Walking back to my desk I felt a knot in my stomach; I kept replaying, “Did I just jeopardize the session?” Since then I go for something lighter—usually Grey Vetiver—or skip fragrance entirely when I’m sitting inches away from users.

On the flip side, my younger sister once hugged me at a family dinner, caught a whiff of Oud Wood, and said it reminded her of the cedar boxes our grandparents stored tea in. Watching her face soften like that made me realize scent can be a quiet bridge to memory. I still reach for Oud Wood when I’m heading to see family; it feels like bringing a shared story with me.

So compliments or discomfort—both shape my choices. Now I ask myself, “Who will be in my radius, and what do I want them to feel?”

history.question: Looking back on your experiences with perfumes, is there anything that stands out as particularly surprising or unexpected?
history.answer:
Two moments still catch me off guard when I think about my perfume habits.

First, the Oud Wood incident. I’d just bought the bottle, felt invincible, sprayed four times before a Monday stakeholder review. Half-way through the meeting the CFO leaned over and whispered, “Great deck, but the room smells like an incense shop.” I was mortified. Up to that point I’d assumed projection was linear—more sprays = longer longevity, same perception. Turns out tropical humidity amplifies heavier woods. That single comment made me pull back and start testing every fragrance on skin in real-world settings: commute, elevator, cramped meeting room. I still like Oud Wood, but now it’s strictly a one-spray, end-of-day scent. The surprise was learning my “personal” choice wasn’t personal at all; everyone around me was a silent stakeholder.

The second was how scent memory can blindside me. I rotated in Bois Marocain during a sprint week because I wanted something dry and grounding. On day three, a wave of nostalgia hit—my grandfather’s mah-jong room in Kuala Lumpur, lacquered wood and cigar smoke. I hadn’t smelled that in twenty years. The emotional punch was so strong I couldn’t focus for a good hour. I’d always thought I picked perfumes rationally: notes, longevity, brand. Realizing an aroma could teleport me like that challenged the neat taxonomy I’d built in my head. Now I keep a small journal, jotting not just accords but any mood or memory that surfaces. It slows my purchasing cycle, but it’s worth it.

Both moments—over-projecting in that meeting and being ambushed by memory—remind me I’m still learning. Fragrance isn’t static data; it’s context, environment, subconscious wiring. Accepting that unpredictability keeps the ritual interesting and, honestly, keeps me humble.

history.question: Can you tell me about the last time you bought or considered buying a perfume?
history.answer:
About eight months ago I was packing for a close friend’s wedding in Sydney and realised the cologne I’d had for years was basically air. On a lunch break I ducked into the Bourke Street Myer to replace it. 

The moment I hit the fragrance floor I felt a bit stranded—strong lights, competing music tracks, every brand spritzing the air. Descriptions like “woody-oriental” or “aromatic marine” meant nothing once my nose was overloaded. Three paper strips in, I couldn’t tell one from the next.  

What really stuck with me was the packaging waste: thick glass, plastic caps, foil-lined boxes. I asked a sales assistant if any brand offered refills or recycled glass. She pointed to a niche label that did, but the price was north of $200. My gut reaction was, “I won’t spray away that much money, especially when I’ll only use it a couple of times a week.” So I walked out empty-handed.  

That night, back home, I spent half an hour online digging for an Australian company that listed full ingredients and used refillable bottles. Ended up ordering a 30 mL bergamot-and-cedar scent from a Byron Bay outfit. Cardboard sleeve, no plastic, and they give a discount when you send the bottle back. Price was still higher than a mainstream brand, but I felt better about the environmental side and the transparency.  

The whole episode reminded me how jargon and sensory overload can drive a buyer away, even when they enter the store ready to spend. If the sustainable option had been easier to spot on the shelf, I’d probably have bought on the spot instead of going online later.

history.question: What usually prompts you to look for a new fragrance?
history.answer:
Two things push me. First, when the bottle that lives on my dresser is down to its last few sprays, I treat that as a checkpoint rather than an automatic repurchase. I’ll ask myself, “Has this scent still felt like me in client meetings and site visits?” If the answer’s no—maybe it now feels a bit too heavy in Melbourne’s summer—then I start hunting.

The second is feedback, explicit or subtle. Last year a junior architect said, almost in passing, that the cedar note I was wearing reminded her of her grandfather’s after-shave. I laughed it off, but on the drive home it bothered me more than I expected. That single comment made me realise I’d drifted into a scent that read older than I wanted. I spent the next weekend sampling lighter, greener options with recyclable packaging; the sustainability angle mattered as much as the smell.

So it’s usually either the bottle running dry or a moment when someone’s reaction tells me the fragrance no longer matches how I want to show up professionally.

history.question: Can you walk me through what happens from the moment you decide you want a perfume to actually making the purchase?
history.answer:
The trigger is almost always practical—my everyday scent runs low and I catch myself tilting the bottle, hoping for one more spray. From that point the process splits into two phases: desk research and sensory testing.

Phase 1 – desk research  
I open a note in Notion and list three things: longevity, ingredients transparency, and whether the brand does refillable bottles. I’ll spend an evening on Reddit fragrance threads and a couple of Australian review sites, skimming comments for phrases like “projects for eight hours” or “goes musky after lunch.” What still trips me up is the language—terms like “gourmand” or “animalic” feel abstract, so I keep a running glossary for myself. By the end of the night I usually have four candidates and a bit of price shock; niche brands creep past $250, which stings.

Phase 2 – sensory testing  
The next Saturday I drive to the Myer in Melbourne CBD. The counter experience is the stressful bit. After the fourth strip my nose just…flattens; every scent blurs. I’ll ask for samples to take home, but staff turnover means policies change—some days they hand them out, other days it’s a hard no and a polite smile. When they do agree, I label the vials, wear one per day, and jot notes—“cedar kicks in at 2 p.m., still present after gym.” That small ritual feels almost scientific and, honestly, satisfying.

Decision point  
By mid-week I’ve lived with each option long enough to know which sits well on my skin. The winner usually isn’t the flashiest top note but the one that still feels like me after dinner. I’ll price-check again online; if the gap is more than 15 percent I order from an authorized web store, otherwise I circle back to the counter—partly loyalty, partly wanting to see the bottle before handing over the card.

The emotional arc is a mix of curiosity and mild fatigue. The research energises me, but the in-store overload and the fear of a costly blind buy still make me pause. When I finally tap my card I’m relieved more than excited—relieved that the scent matches the spreadsheets in my head and won’t end up gathering dust on the shelf.

history.question: When you try different perfumes, how do you notice their effect on your mood or energy?
history.answer:
I usually catch the difference within the first ten minutes. If I spray a bright, citrus-heavy sample—think bergamot or grapefruit—my shoulders come up, my cadence picks up a notch, and I’m suddenly planning the rest of the afternoon instead of crawling toward it. One afternoon after a five-hour stretch in CAD, I tried a small vial of Atelier’s Orange Sanguine; I’d meant to save it for later, but I was fading. Two breaths in, I was sitting straighter, tapping the keyboard quicker. It wasn’t caffeine, but the effect felt similar—like an ambient nudge rather than a jolt.

Woody or resinous scents hit me differently. A vetiver-amber blend I’ve been testing lately lands low in the chest; my breathing slows and the studio chatter almost fades into the background. That’s useful when I need to comb through drawings for errors—steady focus, no rush. The downside is it can bleed into lethargy if I overapply; I caught myself rereading the same spec sheet three times because I’d gone a bit heavy on the wrist spray.

The tricky bit is olfactory fatigue. After three or four trials my nose taps out, and then mood signals get fuzzy—I think I feel something, but I’m mostly riding on expectation. I’ve started limiting tests to one in the morning, one late afternoon, so I can link scent to energy shift with some honesty. Still learning, but those distinct moments—citrus lift, woody grounding—are clear enough that they influence which bottle I reach for before a design review versus a late-night render session.

history.question: Can you recall a time when a fragrance influenced how you felt during the day?
history.answer:
Last winter I grabbed a small decant of a bright neroli-based scent—kind of a crisp, sun-lit citrus with a bit of white floral. I’d been up late debugging a finicky CAD script, so I started the next morning groggy, already dreading a design review with a client who’s, you know, famously detail-obsessed. I sprayed that fragrance while I was packing my laptop. Within a few minutes the sharp citrus hit woke me up more than the coffee. Walking to the car I noticed I was literally breathing deeper; the air felt clearer. 

The real shift happened in the meeting room. Usually I’m hyper-focused on slide order and structural tolerances, but that scent kept nudging me into a lighter headspace—almost playful. I found myself explaining a sustainability trade-off with a bit more warmth than usual, and the client actually smiled instead of diving straight into numbers. It wasn’t data, obviously, but I could feel the room soften. By lunch I realised I’d moved through a three-hour review without that usual tension in my shoulders.

Flip side: a month later I tested a heavier oud on a site visit—thought it would project confidence. Instead, in the cramped elevator with contractors, it felt oppressive. I caught a wrinkle on a foreman’s face and suddenly worried I smelled like I was covering something up. Spent the rest of the day distracted, second-guessing every comment I made about load paths. That taught me the hard way that projection and context matter as much as the notes themselves.

So yeah, same basic routine—spray, drive, meetings—but the fragrance either lifted me into a calmer, more collaborative mode or dragged me into self-conscious overthinking. It’s a bigger lever on mood than I expected.

history.question: What sort of feelings or states do you hope to experience when choosing a perfume?
history.answer:
Mostly I’m chasing two things. First is a kind of grounded focus. When I’m deep in a model for six hours straight, I don’t want something loud; I want a subtle cedar-vetiver note that makes me feel steady, almost like I’m back in my grandfather’s shed where everything smelled of sawdust and fresh timber. That hint of wood settles my nerves and keeps my mind clear enough to catch the small flaws before they snowball.

The second is quiet confidence for client meetings. A touch of bergamot or light amber gives me that extra lift—nothing flashy, just enough so I catch the scent when I adjust my collar and think, “Right, I’ve got this.” There was a morning last year when I wore a heavier, sweeter fragrance by mistake; halfway through the presentation I felt distracted, even self-conscious. That moment reminded me how scent can either anchor me or pull me off balance, so now I’m careful: I test a strip while sketching, wait an hour, and only then decide. I’m still experimenting, honestly, but when the blend hits that calm-plus-confidence sweet spot, the whole day flows.

history.question: Have you ever avoided or stopped using a perfume because of the way it made you feel?
history.answer:
Yes. A couple of years ago I bought a cedar-and-leather fragrance thinking it would project confidence during client meetings. On paper it smelled refined; on my skin it turned almost smoky, almost claustrophobic. The first morning I wore it I had back-to-back design reviews that were already tense because of budget overruns. About an hour in, the scent felt like an extra layer of pressure—thick, insistent, hard to escape. I caught myself breathing shallowly, almost bracing against it, and that amplified the stress in the room.

I tried it twice more, hoping it was just context, but each time the same heaviness crept in. The perfume started to anchor itself to that sense of being cornered by timelines and resistant stakeholders. After the third attempt I shelved the bottle. I still like cedar in theory, but the emotional association is too strong; even catching a hint of it on a scarf nudges me back to that cramped meeting room.

What I learned is that fragrance can cement a moment, good or bad, far more vividly than I’d expected. Now I test new scents on quieter days first, giving myself space to notice how they sit with my mood before bringing them into high-stakes settings.

history.question: When you reflect on the perfumes you've owned, are there any scents that stood out for their impact on your motivation or confidence?
history.answer:
Two come to mind.

First is Terre d’Hermès. I bought it when we were knee-deep in that software-integration fiasco. Most days I felt like I was dragging a boulder uphill—budget spreadsheets open, colleagues grumbling about broken plug-ins. The scent’s dry citrus and earthy vetiver hit just after the morning coffee; it snapped me into a clearer headspace. I’d catch a whiff while troubleshooting compatibility errors and, weirdly, it reminded me why I’d pushed for the tool in the first place—progress, bigger picture, all that. It didn’t solve the blockers, but it nudged my mindset from defensive to problem-solving. I noticed I volunteered ideas more readily in stand-ups. Once the bottle ran out, my motivation dipped a touch, enough that I realised the fragrance had become a tiny ritual of “reset” before the chaos.

The other is Tom Ford Oud Wood. I wore it the day I confronted the architect about that structural flaw in the Epping project. Walking into the meeting, palms clammy, timeline on the line—one spray felt like armour. The smoky, resinous note stayed with me through the tense back-and-forth. I could feel my posture straighten each time the scent rose off my collar. The confidence boost wasn’t placebo; I spoke slower, held eye contact, and the team eventually agreed to the redesign. Since then I save that scent for high-stakes presentations. The downside: it’s heavy, almost imposes on the space, so I’m hyper-aware of wearing it in tight site offices; too much and I worry about overpowering people, which pulls me out of the confident state I’m after.

Everything else on my shelf—fresh aquatics, a couple of niche gourmands—never moved the needle much. They smell pleasant but they don’t anchor an emotion. I’m still hunting for something lighter than Oud Wood yet just as grounding, without the environmental concerns around exotic woods. That search is ongoing.

history.question: How do you usually decide which scent to wear on a particular day?
history.answer:
First thing in the morning I check my calendar while the kettle’s boiling. If the day involves client reviews or site walks, I reach for something light—usually a citrus-leaning cologne. On a muddy construction site a heavy amber feels out of place, and a bright scent helps me stay alert when I’m squinting at rebar details.

When I’m desk-bound modeling all afternoon, mood matters more than context. If I’m anxious about a tricky geometry problem, I’ll pick a dry vetiver that feels almost meditative. There’s a specific bottle—Terre d’Hermès—that I keep near the monitor; one spray and the earthy note reminds me of that moment years ago when I caught the structural flaw. It’s like a quiet cue to slow down and look closer.

The hardest choice is big presentation days. Part of me wants the boost of something bolder, but I’ve misjudged intensity before and spent the meeting worrying I smelled like I was trying too hard. Now I do a quick wrist test, open the window, come back in five minutes, and see if the scent still feels like background instead of broadcast. If it passes that “background” test, I’m good.

So, mood first, agenda second, and a short pause to make sure the fragrance supports the work rather than compete with it.

history.question: What role, if any, do memories or associations play when you select a perfume?
history.answer:
Memories drive most of my choices. If I’m reaching for Terre d’Hermès before a client review, it’s less about the notes on the box and more about a very specific afternoon ten years ago. I’d just flagged that structural flaw in the Epping development—the one that could have derailed the whole build—and the lead architect shook my hand outside the site office. The wind carried this dry, mineral-woody smell from the surrounding gum trees, and later, when I tested Terre, the flinty orange-cedar accord took me straight back to that moment. Now, whenever I need to channel that same steadiness under pressure, I spray it once and let the association do half the psychological work.

There’s a softer side, too. On quieter weekends I’ll wear L’Artisan’s Mémoire de Roses because it reminds me of sitting in Mum’s garden sketching facade ideas during uni breaks. The first whiff of bright raspberry-rose knocks the edge off my usual analytical mode and nudges me toward looser, more exploratory thinking—useful when I’m ideating sustainability concepts without the weight of deadlines.

So the bottle isn’t just fragrance; it’s a shortcut to emotional states tied to pivotal memories. If a scent doesn’t anchor to something meaningful, it rarely survives the next wardrobe purge, no matter how technically “good” it is.

history.question: Have friends or family ever commented on your scent choices? If so, how did that affect your decisions?
history.answer:
Yeah, a couple of moments stand out.  

About five years ago a teammate pulled me aside after a tight review meeting and said, “Mate, your cologne’s a bit loud in that small room.” I’d honestly never thought about projection before; I’d just grabbed what I liked that morning. I remember feeling a mix of embarrassment and gratitude—embarrassed because I might’ve distracted people, grateful because he was candid. The next day I switched to something lighter and started doing a quick “one-spray, walk-through” instead of the full wrist-neck routine. Since then I always test a new scent in the car on the way to work with the windows up—if it feels heavy, I save it for weekends.

On the flip side, my sister once hugged me at a family lunch and said the fragrance reminded her of Dad’s old aftershave. That hit me differently—warm, a bit nostalgic—so I kept that particular scent in rotation for family gatherings. It’s less about the scent itself now and more about the little bit of shared memory it sparks each time.

Those two comments—one constructive, one sentimental—pretty much recalibrated how I think about wearing fragrance. Now I weigh context and the people around me just as much as personal preference.

history.question: Looking back on your experiences with perfumes, is there anything that stands out as particularly surprising or unexpected?
history.answer:
One moment stays with me. A year ago I was testing a vetiver-heavy fragrance—picked it because the dry-down reminded me of freshly planed hardwood, something I associate with early site visits. I wore it to a kickoff meeting, expecting nobody to notice. Mid-discussion the site foreman paused, sniffed the air, and said the scent reminded him of his late father’s workshop. He got visibly emotional for a second, and the whole room shifted; the mood softened, conversation turned more personal, and decisions that usually drag on wrapped up in half an hour.  

What surprised me wasn’t the compliment—it was how a scent I chose for private, almost technical reasons triggered someone else’s memory so intensely. I’d always framed fragrance as a personal finishing touch, almost like a polished pair of shoes. That meeting forced me to acknowledge the social dimension: aroma leaks into shared space and can nudge dynamics in ways I can’t predict or fully control.  

The flip side happened later. I tried a citrus-amber blend a colleague recommended. On my skin it ballooned—by lunchtime even I found it cloying. A junior designer finally joked that the office “smelled like a hotel lobby.” I realised I’d over-indexed on external feedback without testing longevity in real conditions. Since then I decant samples into tiny atomisers and wear them on a long workday before committing.  

So, yeah, the unexpected part is how something as intangible as perfume can both open doors emotionally and, when I misjudge it, distract from the work. I pay more attention now, but I’m still learning where that invisible line sits.
